caption:
Barclays will cut about 5,000 jobs this year, roughly 5 percent of its workforce.
About 60 percent of the cuts hit support roles, and the bank says AI means it needs fewer developers.
Around 1,000 roles are already gone, with the rest set to go by year end.

Would you still want to be a developer at a big bank right now?

paragraphs.text: Barclays plans to cut about 5,000 roles in 2026, roughly 5 percent of its global workforce, the UK bank said on October 22, 2026, alongside its third quarter results. According to Reuters, the bank is using technology including artificial intelligence to lower its fixed costs.

Finance chief Anna Cross said about 1,000 of those roles have already been eliminated and that the remainder will go by the end of the year, Reuters reported. AFP reported that the reductions are scheduled to be completed by the end of 2026.

About 60 percent of the job losses relate to support functions, the bank said. Computer Weekly reported that Barclays tied part of the reduction to needing fewer developers as AI makes its staff more productive. AFP said the bank described the cuts as a mix of organizational simplification and efficiency from technology change driven by AI.

Barclays expects 1.1 billion pounds in efficiency savings in 2027, with the measures it has taken expected to remove 5,000 full time positions, according to Computer Weekly. Reuters reported that the bank booked a further 201 million pounds in structural cost actions during the third quarter as part of a longer plan to bring down expenses, including staff costs.

Speaking at a results meeting, Chief Executive C.S. Venkatakrishnan said the cuts were the result of technology investments. "AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future," he said, according to Computer Weekly. He described AI as "the icing on the cake" rather than the cake itself, arguing that banks first need to build the underlying infrastructure to get its benefits.

The job plan came with quarterly results that fell short of analyst expectations. Reuters reported third quarter profit of 2.3 billion pounds, up from a year earlier, with weakness in fixed income trading as the main drag. Fixed income revenue fell 19 percent to 1 billion pounds against forecasts of 1.3 billion pounds, while equities revenue rose 47 percent.

AFP reported that profit after tax rose to 1.65 billion pounds from 1.46 billion pounds a year earlier and that total group income rose 3 percent to 7.37 billion pounds. Venkatakrishnan said he was disappointed with the fixed income performance and that it would get his attention, according to Reuters.

Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, told AFP that the bank failed to match expectations in the quarter. He also pointed to an expected increase in sector tax in the coming UK budget and a reported probe into the way risks in the bank's private credit portfolio were presented.

Barclays is not alone. Computer Weekly reported that HSBC said earlier in October that it plans to cut half of its management and specialist roles in wealth management and reduce its human financial advisers by 70 percent, using AI in their place.

The Barclays announcement is notable for how directly it names software development as an area where AI reduces headcount. Banks have long cited automation in cost programs, but singling out developers suggests AI coding tools are now part of how large employers plan their workforce, not only how they plan their software.
The next signal to watch is whether other large banks and employers tie specific job counts to AI in their own results, and whether Barclays reaches its 1.1 billion pound savings target in 2027.
